keyTerms: Trait — a feature or quality
Inherited trait — passed from parents through genes
Learned trait — gained by practice or from surroundings
Gene — tiny instruction in our cells that passes traits on

check.q: Which of these is an inherited trait?
check.why: Earlobe shape is passed on through genes, while languages and skills are learned.

sections.md:
Here is a fun class survey the chapter suggests in spirit. Ask every classmate to try three things:

1. **Roll the tongue** into a 'U' shape.
2. **Check earlobes** in a mirror — do they hang free, or are they joined to the cheek?
3. **Fold hands** with fingers locked — is your left thumb on top, or your right?

Make a tally table on the board. Suppose a class of 40 found: tongue-rollers 28, non-rollers 12. Check: 28 + 12 = 40. ✔ So more than half — 28 out of 40 — can roll their tongues.

Now ask at home: can your parents do it? Often (not always) tongue-rolling runs in families. Scientists now say it is partly learned too — some people learn it with practice! This shows how tricky it is to sort traits.

> **Think:** Is any trait in your class shared by *everyone*? Is any trait shared by *no one*?

check.q: In a class of 36, 21 have free earlobes. How many have attached earlobes?
check.why: 36 − 21 = 15 children have attached earlobes.

sections.md:
Let's sort some traits:

**Inherited (born with):** eye colour, hair type, skin tone, dimples, blood group, earlobe shape, natural height range.

**Learned (picked up):** language, cooking, dancing, swimming, handwriting, good manners, favourite food, religion and customs, a love of music or maths.

Some things are **a mix**: height depends on genes **and** on good food and exercise. Musical talent may run in families, but without practice, no one becomes a musician!

So if your father is a great cook, you don't automatically become one — he must **teach** you, and you must practise. And a daughter can learn anything her father knows — farming, carpentry, driving, running a shop — just as a son can.

check.q: Ananya speaks Marathi like her mother. Is this inherited or learned?
check.why: Language is learned by hearing and speaking with people around us, not passed through genes.

sections.md:
About 160 years ago, in a monastery garden in what is now the Czech Republic, a monk named **Gregor Mendel** wanted to know *how* traits pass on. He grew thousands of **pea plants** over about eight years.

He noticed that pea plants were tall or short, had purple or white flowers, round or wrinkled seeds. When he crossed a **tall** plant with a **short** one, **all** the children were tall! But when those children were crossed with each other, some **short** plants appeared again in the next generation — about **1 in 4**.

Mendel realised that each plant carries **two 'factors'** for each trait (one from each parent). One may hide the other, but the hidden one can reappear in grandchildren. Today we call these factors **genes**. He published his work in **1866**, but its importance was understood only around 1900. He is called the **'Father of Genetics'**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#f1f8e9'/><g stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round'><line x1='170' y1='100' x2='170' y2='20'/><line x1='430' y1='100' x2='430' y2='70'/><line x1='300' y1='200' x2='300' y2='130'/><line x1='120' y1='310' x2='120' y2='240'/><line x1='240' y1='310' x2='240' y2='240'/><line x1='360' y1='310' x2='360' y2='240'/></g><line x1='480' y1='310' x2='480' y2='280' stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><g font-size='13'><text x='130' y='115'>tall parent</text><text x='390' y='115'>short parent</text><text x='240' y='215'>all children tall</text><text x='90' y='255'>tall</text><text x='210' y='255'>tall</text><text x='330' y='255'>tall</text><text x='455' y='275' fill='#c62828'>short again!</text></g><g stroke='#999' stroke-dasharray='4 4'><line x1='170' y1='105' x2='300' y2='125'/><line x1='430' y1='105' x2='300' y2='125'/><line x1='300' y1='220' x2='120' y2='240'/><line x1='300' y1='220' x2='480' y2='270'/></g></svg>
fig.caption: Mendel's peas: a hidden trait (shortness) returns in about 1 of 4 grandchildren.
fig.alt: Pea plants: tall and short parents give all tall children; their children are three tall and one short.

check.q: What did Mendel study to learn about inheritance?
check.why: Mendel grew and crossed thousands of pea plants to see how traits pass between generations.

sections.md:
Resemblance is everywhere in nature:

- **Puppies** look like their parent dogs; a **calf** like its mother cow.
- A **mango** seed grows into a mango tree, never a neem tree!
- Farmers choose **seeds from the best plants** — the sweetest, biggest, healthiest — so the next crop has those traits. This is how many crop varieties and animal breeds (like **Gir** and **Sahiwal** cows) were developed over centuries.

But there are **differences** too: no two kittens in a litter look exactly alike. Variety helps living things survive changes.

> **Did you know?** Seedless grapes and watermelons are grown from cuttings or special crosses — people chose and kept those traits on purpose.

The chapter's title is a twist on an old saying, *'Like father, like son'*. Why do we often hear 'son' but not 'daughter'? In many families, a father's work — farming, a shop, a craft — was passed only to sons. Daughters were not taught.

But daughters can inherit traits **and** learn skills from both parents equally. Many daughters have carried forward their fathers' work: pilots, doctors, tabla players, farmers, wrestlers. (The Phogat sisters of Haryana learnt wrestling from their father, Mahavir Singh Phogat, and won medals for India.)

So whatever you inherit, what you **become** depends a lot on what you **learn, practise and choose**.

**Talk about it:** Which skill would you like to learn from someone in your family? Who in your family has learned something that nobody before them knew?

check.q: What decides whether a daughter can carry on her father's work?
options: Whether she is taught and gets to practise
check.why: Skills are learned, so a daughter can do her father's work if she is taught and given the chance to practise.

parts.md: Meher's Abba ran a small repair shop in Lucknow. Every evening she sat on a stool, watching him fix fans and mixers. 'You have my long fingers,' he joked, 'but fingers alone don't fix motors.'

So he started teaching her: which wire is earth, how to test a coil, why you switch off the mains first. She made mistakes, burnt a fuse, and tried again. Her brother preferred cricket; Meher preferred circuits.
Years later, a sign hung over the shop: 'Repairs — Abba & Meher'. Customers said, 'Like father, like daughter!' Meher smiled. The fingers she was born with; the skill she had earned.

summary: Children resemble parents and grandparents in many features.
Inherited traits pass through genes: eye colour, hair type, dimples, earlobes, blood group.
Learned traits come from practice and surroundings: language, skills, habits.
Some traits like height depend on both genes and food/exercise.
A child gets half its genes from the mother and half from the father.
A hidden trait can skip a generation and reappear in grandchildren.
Class surveys (tongue-rolling, earlobes) show how traits vary.
Identical twins share genes but have different fingerprints.
Gregor Mendel studied pea plants and is called the Father of Genetics (work published 1866).
Plants and animals pass traits too; farmers select the best seeds and animals.
Daughters can learn and carry forward any skill, just like sons.
practice: Write five traits you share with a family member.
What is the difference between inherited and learned traits? Give three examples of each.
Can a trait skip a generation? Explain.
Do a tongue-rolling survey of 10 people at home or school and show the tally.
What did Mendel find when he crossed tall and short pea plants?
Is height only inherited? Explain.
Why do farmers save seeds from their best plants?
Why do you think the chapter is called 'Like Father, Like Daughter'?
Name a skill you have learned from an elder in your family.

rd-school-c5-evs-d.ch22-on-the-move-agai.title: On the Move Again
rd-school-c5-evs-d.ch22-on-the-move-agai.subtitle: Every October, whole families pack up and travel to cut sugarcane. What happens to the children's school?

sections.h: The bullock carts leave at dawn
sections.md:
It's October in a dry village in **Maharashtra**. The monsoon was weak, the small field gave only a little jowar, and the family owes money to the moneylender. One morning, bullock carts and trucks line up. Families load pots, quilts, a few clothes, a goat, and the children climb on top. They're going hundreds of kilometres away to **cut sugarcane** for the next six months.

Ten-year-old **Jadhav** (let's call him that) has made this trip every year since he was small. He likes his teacher, but each year he misses half the school year. When he returns in April, he's fallen behind.

This chapter is about **seasonal migration** — people moving to another place for a part of each year to find work. We'll learn:

- the boy's story, scene by scene
- why families migrate
- life in a sugarcane camp
- how sugar is made
- the effect on children's education
- what is being done to help

The chapter is told through a boy from a cane-cutting family. In our own words:

**At home.** The boy lives with his parents and younger sister. The family's field is small and depends on rain. After a poor monsoon there is little to eat and a debt to repay.

**The contractor.** A man from the sugar factory area visits and gives the father an advance. Now the family must go and work it off.

**The journey.** The family travels in a crowded cart with neighbours. The boy is sad to leave school and his friends, but also curious about the road.

**At the fields.** His parents rise before dawn. The boy cares for his little sister, fetches water, and sometimes helps tie bundles. Nights are cold; the hut lets in the wind.

**Coming back.** In summer they return. The father has repaid the loan but saved very little. The boy goes back to school and finds his classmates far ahead. He wonders: *will it be the same next year?*

The meaning: a family can work hard all season and still not escape debt, and the child pays the price in lost schooling. For the original chapter, use the official NCERT link below.

check.q: Why does the boy fall behind in school?
options: He goes with his family for months during the cane season
check.why: The cane season falls in the middle of the school year, so he misses months of classes.

sections.md:
In many villages, there's farm work only in the **rainy season**. If the land is small, dry, or the rains fail, families can't earn enough. They often take **loans** for seeds, illness, weddings or food.

A **mukadam** (labour contractor) comes and offers an **advance** (money paid before the work): 'Come cut cane for the factory this season.' The family accepts — it pays off their old debt and they'll work it back in the cane fields.

In India, lakhs of people migrate seasonally:

| Work | Where people often go |
|---|---|
| Sugarcane cutting | Western Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat |
| Brick kilns | Near big cities, many states |
| Construction | Big cities |
| Salt pans | Gujarat (Little Rann of Kutch) |
| Fish processing, farm harvests | Coastal states, Punjab |

They usually travel as **whole families**, because husband and wife work as a pair: one cuts, the other ties and carries the cane.

check.q: Why do many families from dry villages migrate for part of the year?
options: There is not enough work or income at home
check.why: With small dry farms and failed rains, families must travel to find paid work and repay loans.

sections.md:
At the sugarcane fields, families live in small **huts called *kopi***, made of cane leaves, sticks and plastic sheets, often near the factory or the fields.

A day might look like this:

- Wake up around **3–4 a.m.**, cook bhakri, and go to the fields while it's cool.
- Cut cane with a sharp **koyta** (sickle), strip the leaves, tie bundles.
- Load bundles onto **bullock carts, tractors or trucks** to the factory — sometimes working late into the night.
- Children often look after younger siblings, cook or help tie cane.

Problems: no proper toilets or clean water, cold winter nights in open huts, cuts and injuries, snakes in fields, and **no school** nearby. Payment is by the **tonne** of cane cut, so everyone works long hours.

The cane tops and leaves are used as fodder for the bullocks.

keyTerms: Seasonal migration — moving for work for part of each year
Advance — money paid before work is done
Mukadam — labour contractor
Koyta — sickle used to cut cane

check.q: Why do both husband and wife usually go to cut cane?
options: They work as a pair — one cuts, one ties and carries
check.why: Cane cutting is done in pairs, so contractors hire couples and the whole family travels together.

sections.md:
What happens to the cane at the factory?

1. Cane is **weighed** at the factory gate (payment depends on this).
2. It's **crushed** between heavy rollers to squeeze out **juice**.
3. The juice is **cleaned** and **boiled** to remove water and make it thick.
4. As it cools, **sugar crystals** form.
5. The crystals are separated from the leftover syrup (**molasses**) in spinning machines, dried and packed.

Nothing is wasted: the crushed fibre (**bagasse**) is burned as fuel for the factory's boilers or used for paper; molasses is used to make other products.

In villages, cane juice is also boiled in big open pans to make **gur (jaggery)**.

> **Did you know?** India is one of the world's largest producers of sugar, along with Brazil.

items.what: Weigh the cane
Crush to get juice
Clean and boil the juice
Crystals form as it cools
Spin, dry and pack sugar

fig.caption: Steps in a sugar factory.

check.q: What is bagasse?
options: Crushed cane fibre left after juice is squeezed out
check.why: Bagasse is the dry fibre left after crushing cane, often burned as fuel in the factory.

sections.md:
The cane season runs from about **October/November to April/May** — the middle of the school year. When children go with their parents:

- they **miss months of classes**
- they come back and find they've **fallen behind**, and some feel ashamed and stop going
- older children start working early
- many girls get married young

The **Right to Education Act (2009)** says every child aged **6 to 14** has the right to free and compulsory education. So what can be done?

- **Seasonal hostels** in home villages, so children can stay back with grandparents and attend school.
- **Schools at work sites** — some NGOs and governments run classes near sugar factories and brick kilns.
- **Education guarantee cards** — children carry a card so a school near the work site can admit them.
- **Mobile teachers and learning centres**.

At Jadhav's camp, a teacher runs a tent school in the afternoon. He's learning to read Marathi with other cane-cutters' children.

check.q: According to the Right to Education Act, which children have the right to free schooling?
check.why: The RTE Act (2009) gives every child aged 6 to 14 the right to free and compulsory education.

sections.md:
What could make life better for migrant families?

- More **work in their own villages** (for example, under **MGNREGA**, which promises up to 100 days of paid work a year to rural households).
- **Water conservation** so farms do better in dry years.
- **Fair wages** and written records of work and payment.
- **Housing, toilets, water and health care** at work sites.
- **Ration cards that work anywhere** (*One Nation One Ration Card*), so families get food grain wherever they go.
- **Schooling that moves with the child.**

Think of the sugar in your tea. Many hands — often of families on the move — made it possible.

check.q: How does 'One Nation One Ration Card' help migrant families?
options: They can get ration food grain wherever they are working
check.why: It lets families collect subsidised food grain from ration shops in any state where they are working.

sections.md:
**Talk about it**
- Has anyone in your class moved from another town or state? What was hard about it?
- What would you miss most if you had to leave home for six months every year?

**Find out**
- Which crops in your state need many workers at harvest time? Where do those workers come from?
- Ask a shopkeeper: where does the sugar and gur he sells come from?

**Write**
- Imagine you are the boy. Write a diary page for one day in the cane camp.
- Write a letter to the Collector suggesting two ways to help children of migrant families study.

> **Did you know?** A tonne is 1,000 kg. So 2 tonnes of cane a day means a couple cuts and ties about 2,000 kg — the weight of a small car — every single day!

workedExamples.q: A couple cuts 2 tonnes of cane a day. They are paid ₹350 per tonne. How much do they earn in 25 working days?
They took an advance of ₹15,000. How much is left after repaying it?
The season runs from November to April. How many months is that?
steps: Count: Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr
workedExamples.answer: 6 months

summary: Seasonal migration means moving to another place for work for part of each year.
Families from dry areas of Maharashtra migrate to cut sugarcane from about October to April.
Small, dry farms, failed rains and loans push families to migrate.
A mukadam (contractor) pays an advance that is worked off.
Couples cut and tie cane together; families live in leaf-and-plastic huts called kopi.
Life in camps is hard: very early starts, no toilets, cold nights, injuries.
Sugar is made by crushing cane, boiling juice and crystallising sugar; bagasse is used as fuel.
Children miss months of school and fall behind.
The RTE Act (2009) guarantees free education to children aged 6–14.
Seasonal hostels, work-site schools and education cards help migrant children.
MGNREGA, fair wages and portable ration cards can improve migrant families' lives.

What is an advance? How does it tie a family to the contractor?
Describe a day in a sugarcane-cutting camp.

How does migration affect children's education?

If a new child joined your class from a cane camp, how would you help them?

rd-school-c5-evs-d.revision.title: Class 5 EVS: The Whole Book in One Read
rd-school-c5-evs-d.revision.subtitle: Senses, food, water, shelter, space, forests and journeys, all 22 chapters revised in one go

sections.h: Before we begin: one big question
sections.md:
Why can an ant find a single grain of sugar on your kitchen floor while you walk right past it? Why do people in Ladakh build their houses with thick walls of stone and mud? Why does a farmer in Punjab worry when the water table drops?

Your Class 5 EVS book, *Looking Around*, is really one long answer to one question: **how do living things, people included, depend on the world around them, and on each other?** The 22 chapters fall into six themes:

| Theme | Chapters (in book order) |
|---|---|
| Family and friends: animals, plants, work and play | Super Senses, A Snake Charmer's Story, Seeds and Seeds, Who will do this Work?, Across the Wall, Like Father, Like Daughter |
| Food | From Tasting to Digesting, Mangoes Round the Year, A Seed tells a Farmer's Story |
| Water | Every Drop Counts, Experiments with Water, A Treat for Mosquitoes |
| Travel | Up You Go!, Walls Tell Stories, Sunita in Space |
| Shelter | What if it Finishes...?, A Shelter so High!, When the Earth Shook! |
| Things we make and do | Blow Hot, Blow Cold, No Place for Us?, Whose Forests?, On the Move Again |

(Your book may group a few chapters slightly differently. That's fine: the ideas are what count.)

This read goes theme by theme. Each part ends with a quick check, so you'll know straight away what you remember and what to go back to.

Animals sense the world in ways we can't. In **Super Senses** you met:

- **Ants**, which leave a smell trail and follow it to food and back home.
- **Eagles and kites**, whose eyes are so sharp they can spot a small animal from very high in the sky.
- **Owls**, which see well at night. Their big eyes collect a lot of light.
- **Dogs**, which know each other by smell. They mark their area with urine.
- **Snakes**, which have no ears you can see. They feel vibrations through the ground.
- **Mosquitoes**, which find us by the smell of our sweat and the heat of our bodies.

Some animals sleep through a whole season, like the sloth that sleeps for hours every day, or animals that hibernate in winter.

**A Snake Charmer's Story** is about the Kalbelia community of Rajasthan, who used to earn a living by showing snakes. Laws now protect wild animals, so many have moved on to music and dance. The chapter teaches us that most snakes in India are **not poisonous**. The **big four** that can be dangerous are the cobra, the common krait, the Russell's viper and the saw-scaled viper. A snake does not dance to the been. It follows the movement of the instrument.

> Did you know? Tigers are counted, and protected, in tiger reserves. Animals are endangered when their homes (forests, grasslands) are destroyed.

check.q: How does a snake mostly sense things around it, since it has no outer ears?
options: By feeling vibrations through the ground
check.why: Snakes have no outer ears, so they pick up vibrations from the ground through their bodies.

sections.h: Food: from tongue to stomach to farm
sections.md:
**From Tasting to Digesting.** Different parts of the tongue are often said to pick up sweet, salty, sour and bitter tastes. Saliva begins digesting food in the mouth: chew a piece of roti for a long time and it starts to taste sweet. The food then goes down the food pipe to the stomach, where digestive juices break it down. Glucose gives quick energy, which is why a doctor might give glucose to a weak patient. The chapter also shows how hunger hurts: many children do not get enough to eat. That's why the **mid-day meal** in schools matters.

**Mangoes Round the Year** is about keeping food from spoiling. Food spoils when tiny living things (fungus, bacteria) grow on it. It smells bad, changes colour and grows fluff. We **preserve** food by drying (papad, mango slices), adding salt, oil or sugar (pickles, murabba) and keeping it cool. Aam papad is made by spreading mango pulp in thin layers and drying it in the sun.

**A Seed tells a Farmer's Story** follows a farmer who switched from many local seed varieties and cow-dung manure to bought seeds, chemical fertilisers and tube wells. Crops grew more at first. Later the soil got tired, the water went deeper and costs rose. The chapter asks: how can farming be good for the farmer *and* the land?

check.q: Why does a piece of roti taste sweet if you chew it for a long time?
options: Saliva starts to change the starch into sugar
check.why: Saliva starts digestion in the mouth by breaking starch into simpler sugars, so the taste turns sweet.

sections.md:
**Every Drop Counts** goes to Rajasthan, where rain is scarce. People there built clever ways to store water: **kunds** (covered underground tanks that collect rainwater), **johads**, stepwells (**baoris**) and lakes like **Ghadsisar** in Jaisalmer. Today many old systems have been forgotten as people rely on taps and tube wells. Collecting rainwater from rooftops is called **rainwater harvesting**.

**Experiments with Water** is all about things that float or sink and things that dissolve. Salt and sugar **dissolve** in water. Sand and chalk powder do not. Some things **float** (a dry leaf, a cork), others **sink** (a stone, a coin). An egg sinks in plain water but floats in very salty water. That's also why it's easy to float in the Dead Sea!

**A Treat for Mosquitoes** shows how stagnant water lets mosquitoes breed. Their eggs become larvae in still water. The female *Anopheles* mosquito spreads **malaria**, and the *Aedes* mosquito spreads dengue. A blood test shows malaria, and a medicine treats it. To stop mosquitoes, empty coolers, cover tanks, clear drains and use nets.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='w' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#81d4fa'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#0277bd'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff8e1'/><polygon points='100,120 220,60 340,120' fill='#c62828'/><rect x='120' y='120' width='200' height='110' fill='#ffcc80'/><path d='M340 120 L380 120 L380 230' fill='none' stroke='#607d8b' stroke-width='8'/><rect x='360' y='230' width='160' height='50' rx='8' fill='url(#w)'/><text x='440' y='262' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' fill='#fff' font-family='sans-serif'>Underground tank</text><g fill='#0288d1'><circle cx='150' cy='0' r='4'><animate attributeName='cy' from='0' to='70' dur='1.2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='230' cy='0' r='4'><animate attributeName='cy' from='-20' to='60' dur='1.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='300' cy='0' r='4'><animate attributeName='cy' from='-10' to='95' dur='1.1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='380' cy='130' r='5'><animate attributeName='cy' from='125' to='228' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><text x='220' y='180' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' font-family='sans-serif'>House</text></svg>
fig.caption: Rooftop rainwater harvesting: rain runs off the roof and down a pipe into a tank, the same idea as an old kund.
fig.alt: Rain falling on a roof and flowing through a pipe into an underground tank

check.q: An egg sinks in plain water. What will make it float?
check.why: Salt makes the water denser, so it pushes up harder on the egg and the egg floats.

sections.md:
**Up You Go!** is a mountaineering camp. Students learn to use ropes, carabiners and helmets, cross a river on a rope, and work as a team. In 1984 **Bachendri Pal** became the first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest. Climbers carry less oxygen-rich air with them in their lungs as they go higher, so they climb slowly to let their bodies adjust.

**Walls Tell Stories** takes us to **Golconda Fort** near Hyderabad. Its clever design lets a clap at the gate be heard high up at the top. There were cannons, a moat, water channels and huge gates with spikes against elephants. Old buildings are like history books in stone.

**Sunita in Space** follows astronaut **Sunita Williams**, who has Indian roots, on the International Space Station. From space the Earth looks round, like a ball, and you can't see borders. In space things float because everything, the station included, is falling around the Earth together. Water floats as balls, and astronauts strap themselves in to sleep. On Earth, gravity pulls everything towards the centre, so "down" is always towards the ground wherever you stand on the globe.

check.q: Why do things float inside a space station?
options: The station and everything inside it keep falling around the Earth together
check.why: Everything in the station falls together around the Earth, so nothing presses on the floor and objects seem to float.

sections.md:
**What if it Finishes...?** is about fuels. Petrol, diesel and natural gas come from deep under the ground and took millions of years to form, so they **will run out**. Their smoke pollutes the air. We can save fuel by using buses and trains, cycling, switching off engines at red lights and choosing CNG or electric vehicles.

**A Shelter so High!** shows how houses suit the weather and the materials people have nearby:

| Place | Home | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Ladakh | Thick stone and mud walls, flat roofs | Keeps out the cold; little rain |
| Kashmir | Houseboats, wooden houses with sloping roofs | Lakes; snow slides off the slope |
| Assam/North-East | Bamboo houses on stilts | Heavy rain and floods |
| Rajasthan | Thick mud walls, small windows | Keeps out the heat |
| Changpa (Ladakh) | Rebo tents of yak hair | They move with their herds |

**When the Earth Shook!** remembers the 2001 Gujarat earthquake. It teaches what to do: **Drop, Cover and Hold** under a strong table, keep away from glass, and go to an open space afterwards. Earthquake-safe buildings and a ready emergency kit save lives.

check.q: Why are houses in Assam often built on bamboo stilts?
options: To stay above flood water and damp ground
check.why: Assam gets heavy rain and floods, so raising homes on stilts keeps them dry and safe.

sections.md:
**Blow Hot, Blow Cold** shows that our breath can warm cold hands (blowing slowly from an open mouth) or cool hot tea (blowing fast through rounded lips). The chapter also looks at the stethoscope and how the heartbeat and pulse speed up after running.

**Who will do this Work?** asks why some jobs, like cleaning, are looked down upon. Mahatma Gandhi cleaned toilets himself at his ashram to show that **all work deserves respect**.

**Across the Wall** follows a girls' basketball team that breaks the idea that sport is only for boys. **Like Father, Like Daughter** looks at how traits like dimples or curly hair pass down in families, and how some ideas about girls and boys are unfair.

**No Place for Us?** tells of a family that has to move to the city when a dam floods their village. They end up living in a slum, and the children can't go to school. **Whose Forests?** is about Adivasi people who depend on forests for food, medicine and homes, and their fight for forest rights. Remember the **Chipko** idea of hugging trees to save them. **On the Move Again** is about families who migrate every year, for example to cut sugarcane, and the children who miss school because of it.

1. **Make a theme web.** Write FOOD in the middle and draw lines to everything from the chapters, like saliva, pickles and seeds.
2. **Explain to someone.** Tell a younger cousin why ants walk in a line. If you can teach it, you know it.
3. **Use your own life.** Is there standing water near your home? What fuel does your family use for cooking? EVS questions often ask for *your* experience, and an honest, thoughtful answer scores well.
4. **Map it.** Find Rajasthan, Ladakh, Assam, Gujarat and Hyderabad on a map of India.
5. **Practise long answers** in 3 to 5 clear sentences, with one example each.

check.q: Which of these is a fuel that will one day run out?
check.why: Petrol comes from oil that formed underground over millions of years, so we can use it up far faster than nature makes it.

summary: Animals sense the world in special ways: ants by smell, eagles by sharp sight, snakes by vibrations.
Most Indian snakes are not poisonous; the big four are cobra, krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper.
Digestion starts in the mouth with saliva and continues in the stomach.
Food spoils because of fungus and bacteria; drying, salt, oil, sugar and cooling preserve it.
Rajasthan's kunds, baoris and johads are old forms of rainwater harvesting.
Some things dissolve (salt, sugar) and some don't (sand); salty water helps things float.
Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water; the female Anopheles spreads malaria.
Bachendri Pal was the first Indian woman to climb Everest (1984).
Golconda Fort shows clever old engineering for sound, water and defence.
From space, the Earth looks round with no borders; gravity pulls everything towards Earth's centre.
Petrol and diesel are limited and pollute; save them by using shared and clean transport.
Homes match the climate: stilts in Assam, thick walls in Ladakh and Rajasthan.
During an earthquake: Drop, Cover, Hold.
All work deserves respect; girls and boys should get equal chances.
Dams, migration and forest loss affect people's homes, schooling and rights.

glossary.d: Sleep through a cold season
Keep food from spoiling
Covered tank that stores rainwater
Mix completely into a liquid
Still, not flowing
Move from one place to another to live or work

practice: Name three animals and the special sense each one uses.
Why does food spoil? Write two ways your family preserves food.
What is a kund? Why is it useful in Rajasthan?
List four things you can do to stop mosquitoes breeding near your home.
Why do astronauts float in a space station?
Compare a house in Ladakh with a house in Assam.
What should you do during an earthquake?
Why should all kinds of work be respected? Give an example.
How does a dam sometimes force people to leave their village?
Why do Adivasi communities say the forest belongs to them too?

rd-school-c5-english-a.unit1.title: Unit 1 · Ice-cream Man / Wonderful Waste!
rd-school-c5-english-a.unit1.subtitle: A summer poem about a sweet-seller and a Kerala kitchen story where nothing is wasted

sections.md:
Picture a hot May afternoon. The road shimmers, the dogs sleep in the shade — and then you hear a bell: *tring tring!* Here comes the ice-cream cart!

Unit 1 of *Marigold* (Class 5) pairs two pieces about food and joy:

1. **Ice-cream Man** — a short poem by the American poet **Rachel Field** about an ice-cream seller who brings happiness on summer days.
2. **Wonderful Waste!** — a story set in old Kerala, about a royal cook who turns vegetable leftovers into a famous dish called **avial**.

You will read a full retelling of each, the meaning of every stanza and paragraph, new words, grammar and writing tasks, and practice answers. Rachel Field died in 1942, but because we cannot be sure of the exact wording printed in your book, we explain the poem stanza by stanza in our own words. Read the original free on the NCERT website (link at the end).

check.q: Who wrote the poem 'Ice-cream Man'?
check.why: 'Ice-cream Man' is a poem by the American poet Rachel Field.

sections.md:
**Stanza 1 — the cart arrives.** When summer comes and the streets are dusty and hot, the ice-cream man pushes his cart along. The poet lists the many colours and flavours he carries — chocolate, strawberry, lemon, vanilla. The cart feels like a moving treasure box.

**Stanza 2 — what he sells.** His cart is described as full of good things: cones, cups, sticks and fruit ices of every shade. Children rush out as soon as they hear him. The poet makes us *see* and almost *taste* the colours.

**Stanza 3 — a little fairy-tale.** In a playful line, the poet imagines the cart as something almost magical — like a fountain or a treasure chest — and the ice-cream man is like a king of summer whom the children follow.

**Stanza 4 — the happy ending.** As he moves from street to street, he leaves children smiling and cool. The poet suggests that summer would not be the same without him — he spreads simple joy wherever he goes.

**Central idea:** Small, everyday things — a bell, a cone, a cool treat on a hot day — can bring great happiness. The poem is a cheerful picture of summer in a town.

**Poetic devices:** *rhyme* at the ends of lines, *imagery* of colour and taste, a bouncing *rhythm* like the cart's wheels, and *lists* of flavours.

fig.caption: The ice-cream cart rolls down a hot summer street.
fig.alt: A pink ice-cream cart with a cone on top moving across a sunny road.

check.q: What is the central idea of 'Ice-cream Man'?
options: Simple things bring joy on hot summer days
check.why: The poem celebrates how the ice-cream man spreads cheerful happiness to children in summer.

sections.md:
**Scene 1 — a royal feast.** Long ago, the Maharaja of Travancore (in present-day Kerala) planned a grand feast. Hundreds of guests were invited, and the royal cooks prepared dish after dish on banana leaves.

**Scene 2 — a problem.** Just before the meal, the cook found that one dish was short — there would not be enough to serve everyone. There was no time to make a new dish from fresh vegetables.

**Scene 3 — the clever idea.** The cook looked at the heap of vegetable pieces left over from cutting — ends of drumsticks, carrots, beans, raw banana, yam, gourds — things that would normally be thrown away. He washed them, cut them into long pieces, and cooked them together. He ground coconut, green chillies and garlic into a paste, added it, then curd, and finally poured coconut oil and curry leaves over the top.

**Scene 4 — the surprise.** The new dish was served. The Maharaja and the guests loved it! They asked its name. The cook called it **avial**. From then on, avial became one of the most loved dishes of Kerala, served at the *sadya* (feast) during festivals like Onam.

**Message:** Waste can be turned into something wonderful with a little thought. Using leftovers wisely saves food and money.

**The recipe part:** The lesson also gives the steps for making avial — a good chance to learn *recipe language*: verbs like *cut, wash, boil, grind, add, mix, garnish*, in order.

check.q: What did the cook use to make avial?
check.why: He cooked the leftover vegetable pieces with a coconut paste and curd, inventing avial.

sections.md:
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| feast | a large special meal for many people |
| cart | a small vehicle pushed by hand |
| flavour | the particular taste of food |
| leftover | food or pieces that remain unused |
| grind | to crush into a paste or powder |
| garnish | to decorate food with something on top |
| sadya | a traditional Kerala feast on a banana leaf |
| curd | dahi, thickened milk |

**Opposites:** hot–cold, waste–save, full–empty, sweet–sour.

**Words of taste:** sweet (ice cream), sour (tamarind), salty (chips), bitter (karela), spicy (chillies), tangy (raw mango).

check.q: What does 'garnish' mean?
options: To decorate food with something on top
check.why: Garnish means adding a topping such as curry leaves or coriander to decorate food.

sections.md:
**Countable and uncountable nouns:** We can count *vegetables, cones, carts* (one cone, two cones). We cannot count *water, curd, oil, sugar* — we say *some oil, a cup of curd*.

**Describing words (adjectives) for food:** *creamy* ice cream, *crunchy* papad, *juicy* mango, *hot* soup.

**Writing a recipe:** Use a title, list of ingredients, then numbered steps beginning with action words. For example, a simple *lemon sharbat*:
1. Squeeze one lemon into a glass.
2. Add two spoons of sugar and a pinch of salt.
3. Pour in cold water and stir well.
4. Add ice and serve.

**Speaking:** Talk about a dish that is made from leftovers in your home — like *upma* from stale bread or *khichdi* from leftover rice and dal.

check.q: Which of these is an uncountable noun?
check.why: Water cannot be counted one by one; we say 'some water' or 'a glass of water'.

summary: Unit 1 has a poem, Ice-cream Man, and a story, Wonderful Waste!
Rachel Field's poem shows the ice-cream man bringing joy on hot summer days.
The poem uses rhyme, rhythm and colourful imagery of flavours.
Wonderful Waste! is set at a royal feast in Travancore, Kerala.
A dish fell short, so the cook used leftover vegetable pieces.
He added coconut paste, curd, coconut oil and curry leaves — and invented avial.
Avial is now part of the Kerala sadya, especially at Onam.
The message: waste can become wonderful with thought.
Recipes use action verbs in numbered steps.
Countable nouns can be counted; uncountable nouns (water, oil) cannot.
practice: Why do children love the ice-cream man? Answer in three sentences.
List four flavours or colours you imagine on the ice-cream cart.
What problem did the royal cook face?
How did he solve it? Describe the steps.
Why is the story called 'Wonderful Waste!'?
Write the recipe of your favourite snack in numbered steps.
Sort into countable and uncountable: rice, banana, milk, spoon, salt, plate.
Write a short paragraph: 'How my family avoids wasting food'.

rd-school-c5-english-a.unit2.title: Unit 2 · Teamwork / Flying Together
rd-school-c5-english-a.unit2.subtitle: A poem about working together and a tale of wild geese who escape a hunter by listening to wisdom

sections.md:
Have you ever tried to carry a heavy desk alone? It barely moves. With four friends — one at each corner — it lifts like a feather. That is the big idea of Unit 2.

The unit has:
1. **Teamwork** — a short poem that says that great things are done when people work together.
2. **Flying Together** — a folk tale about a flock of wild geese, a wise old goose, a creeper and a hunter.

Both pieces teach that **cooperation and listening to wise advice** keep us safe and help us succeed. Here you'll find a full retelling, the meaning of each part, word study, grammar and writing practice. Read the original text free on the NCERT website (link at the end).

check.q: What common idea links both pieces in Unit 2?
options: Working together and listening to advice
check.why: Both the poem and the story show that cooperation and good advice lead to success and safety.

sections.md:
**Part 1 — alone is hard.** The poem begins by saying it is fine to want to be the best, but no one can do every job by themselves. A single person, however clever, has limits.

**Part 2 — everyone has a part.** Like players in a team or musicians in a band, each person does one part well. When all the parts fit, the whole becomes far greater than any one member.

**Part 3 — the reward.** The poem ends by saying that when we pull together, we reach goals that seemed impossible, and everyone shares the joy.

**Central idea:** *Together Everyone Achieves More* — success comes from cooperation, not from showing off alone.

**Examples from life:** a cricket team where the bowler, wicket-keeper and fielders each play a role; Indian scientists at ISRO working in thousands of small teams for Chandrayaan-3, which landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023; a family cooking a festival meal together.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='220' fill='#eef9f0'/><rect x='200' y='100' width='200' height='40' fill='#a0522d'><animate attributeName='y' values='120;60;120' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><g fill='#3b7dd8'><circle cx='190' cy='150' r='14'><animate attributeName='cy' values='170;110;170' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='260' cy='150' r='14'><animate attributeName='cy' values='170;110;170' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='340' cy='150' r='14'><animate attributeName='cy' values='170;110;170' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='410' cy='150' r='14'><animate attributeName='cy' values='170;110;170' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><text x='300' y='35' font-size='20' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>Together, the load lifts</text></svg>
fig.caption: Four friends lift a heavy log together.
fig.alt: Four figures rise together, lifting a log.

check.q: According to the poem, why is teamwork important?
options: Each person's part adds up to something greater
check.why: The poem says when each member does their part, the team achieves more than anyone could alone.

sections.md:
**Scene 1 — the tall tree.** A flock of wild geese lived in a tall tree in a forest. Among them was a very old, wise goose who noticed things others ignored.

**Scene 2 — the small creeper.** One day the wise goose saw a small creeper (a climbing plant) growing at the bottom of the tree. He told the others, *"We should destroy this creeper now. One day it will grow and climb the tree, and someone could climb it to reach us."*

**Scene 3 — laughter.** The young geese laughed. *"It is such a small creeper! Why worry?"* They said they would deal with it later and did nothing. The wise goose felt sad but said no more.

**Scene 4 — the creeper grows.** Months passed. The creeper grew thick and strong, winding all the way up the trunk.

**Scene 5 — the hunter.** One morning, when the geese were away looking for food, a hunter climbed up the creeper and set a net/trap in the branches, then left.

**Scene 6 — trapped!** In the evening the geese returned and were caught in the trap. Frightened, they cried, *"We should have listened to you! What do we do now?"*

**Scene 7 — the wise plan.** The old goose said, *"When the hunter comes, pretend to be dead. He will think we are no use alive, take us out, and throw us on the ground. When the last one is thrown, we will all fly away together."*

**Scene 8 — the escape.** The next morning the hunter came. The geese lay still. Thinking they were dead, he took them out one by one and threw them to the ground. When the last one landed, the wise goose gave a signal — and the whole flock rose into the sky together, safe. The surprised hunter could only watch.

**Moral:** *Listen to the wise and experienced*, and *solve small problems before they become big*. Also — working together, the geese escaped.

check.q: Why did the old goose want the creeper destroyed?
options: It would grow and help someone climb the tree
check.why: He foresaw that a grown creeper would let a hunter climb up to their nests.

sections.md:
| Character | What they are like |
|---|---|
| Wise old goose | far-sighted, calm, patient; forgives the others and still helps |
| Young geese | carefree, careless at first, later humble and obedient |
| Hunter | clever but fooled because he trusted appearances |

**Lessons:**
- *A stitch in time saves nine* — fixing a problem early saves trouble.
- Respect the experience of elders.
- In danger, stay calm and act together.

**Think:** Have you seen a small problem grow big? A small leak in a roof during the monsoon, an unfinished homework pile, a tiny cut that was not cleaned?

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#d9eeff'/><rect x='80' y='90' width='26' height='150' fill='#7a4b25'/><circle cx='93' cy='80' r='60' fill='#3c9a4a'/><path d='M93 240 C80 200 110 180 93 140' stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='5' fill='none'/><g fill='#fff' stroke='#555'><g><animateMotion path='M150 180 Q 300 40 560 60' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M0 0 l-18 -8 l8 8 l-8 8z'/></g><g><animateMotion path='M150 190 Q 300 60 560 90' dur='5s' begin='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M0 0 l-18 -8 l8 8 l-8 8z'/></g><g><animateMotion path='M150 200 Q 300 80 560 120' dur='5s' begin='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M0 0 l-18 -8 l8 8 l-8 8z'/></g></g><text x='380' y='220' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>All together — fly!</text></svg>
fig.caption: At the wise goose's signal, the whole flock flies away together.
fig.alt: A tree with a creeper; three geese rise into the sky.

check.q: How did the geese escape?
options: They pretended to be dead and flew off together
check.why: Pretending to be dead, they were thrown down, and when the last one landed they all flew away.

sections.md:
**New words:** *flock* (group of birds), *creeper* (plant that climbs), *trap* (device to catch animals), *wise* (having good judgement), *foolish* (lacking sense), *signal* (a sign to act), *peep* (look quickly).

**Collective nouns:** a *flock* of geese/sheep, a *herd* of cows, a *pack* of wolves, a *swarm* of bees, a *team* of players, a *bunch* of grapes.

**Opposites with un- / dis-:** wise–unwise, happy–unhappy, obey–disobey, agree–disagree.

**Writing:** Write a short story in which a small problem becomes big because no one listened. Begin with a hook, tell the problem, the mistake, the danger and the solution, and end with a moral.

**Speaking:** In groups, act out Flying Together — one wise goose, several young geese and a hunter.

check.q: What is the collective noun for bees?
check.why: A group of bees is called a swarm.

summary: Unit 2 has the poem Teamwork and the story Flying Together.
Teamwork says no one can do everything alone; each part matters.
Teams achieve more than individuals.
In Flying Together, a wise old goose warns about a small creeper.
The young geese laugh and ignore him.
The creeper grows; a hunter climbs it and sets a trap.
The geese are caught and finally ask the wise goose for help.
He tells them to pretend to be dead.
Thrown to the ground, they fly off together at his signal.
Morals: listen to the wise; fix small problems early; act together.
Collective nouns: flock, herd, swarm, pack, team.
practice: Give two examples of teamwork from your school or home.
What did the wise goose see growing at the foot of the tree?
How did the young geese react to his warning?
What did the hunter do?
Describe the plan that saved the geese.
What lesson did the young geese learn?
Write collective nouns for: fish, cows, flowers, soldiers.
Write a paragraph: 'A time when my team succeeded'.

rd-school-c5-english-a.unit3.title: Unit 3 · My Shadow / Robinson Crusoe Discovers a Footprint
rd-school-c5-english-a.unit3.subtitle: Stevenson's playful shadow poem in full, and a lonely island where a single footprint changes everything

sections.md:
Stand in the sun and wave. Something waves back — your shadow! Now imagine you live alone on an island for fifteen years and one day you find a **footprint** in the sand that isn't yours…

Unit 3 has:
1. **My Shadow** by **Robert Louis Stevenson** (1850–1894), from *A Child's Garden of Verses* (1885). Stevenson's work is long out of copyright, so the full poem is given below with an explanation of every stanza.
2. **Robinson Crusoe Discovers a Footprint** — an extract adapted from Daniel Defoe's novel *Robinson Crusoe* (1719). Because your book uses an adapted version, we retell it scene by scene in our own words.

check.q: Who wrote 'My Shadow'?
check.why: 'My Shadow' is from Robert Louis Stevenson's 'A Child's Garden of Verses'.

sections.h: 📜 Full text — My Shadow (R. L. Stevenson)
sections.md:
> I have a little shadow that goes in and out with me,
> And what can be the use of him is more than I can see.
> He is very, very like me from the heels up to the head;
> And I see him jump before me, when I jump into my bed.
>
> The funniest thing about him is the way he likes to grow—
> Not at all like proper children, which is always very slow;
> For he sometimes shoots up taller like an india-rubber ball,
> And he sometimes gets so little that there's none of him at all.
>
> He hasn't got a notion of how children ought to play,
> And can only make a fool of me in every sort of way.
> He stays so close beside me, he's a coward you can see;
> I'd think shame to stick to nursie as that shadow sticks to me!
>
> One morning, very early, before the sun was up,
> I rose and found the shining dew on every buttercup;
> But my lazy little shadow, like an arrant sleepy-head,
> Had stayed at home behind me and was fast asleep in bed.

sections.md:
**Stanza 1.** The child says he has a small shadow that goes *in and out* with him — indoors and outdoors, wherever he goes. He cannot understand what use the shadow is. It looks exactly like him *from the heels up to the head*. When he jumps into bed at night (with a lamp behind him), he sees the shadow jump ahead of him.

**Stanza 2.** The funniest thing is how the shadow grows. Real children grow *very slowly*, but the shadow sometimes *shoots up* tall, like a bouncing rubber ball, and sometimes becomes so small that it almost disappears. (Science: when the light is low — morning, evening — shadows are long; at noon, when the sun is overhead, they are tiny.)

**Stanza 3.** The shadow has no idea how children should play — it just copies him and makes him look silly. It always sticks close to him, so the child calls it a *coward*. He says he would be ashamed to cling to his *nursie* (nanny) the way the shadow clings to him.

**Stanza 4.** One early morning, before sunrise, the child gets up and finds dew shining on the buttercups. But his shadow is not there! He jokes that the lazy *sleepy-head* stayed in bed. (Science: with no sunlight yet, there is no shadow.)

**Central idea:** A child's playful, curious view of his shadow. Without knowing the science, he treats the shadow as a person — that is **personification**.

**Devices:** rhyming couplets (*me/see, head/bed, grow/slow, ball/all, play/way, see/me, up/buttercup, sleepy-head/bed*), simile (*like an india-rubber ball*), humour.

check.q: Why was the shadow 'asleep in bed' in the last stanza?
options: The sun had not risen, so there was no shadow
check.why: Before sunrise there is no bright light to make a shadow — the child playfully imagines it is still asleep.

sections.h: Robinson Crusoe Discovers a Footprint — the story retold
sections.md:
**Background.** Robinson Crusoe was an English sailor who was shipwrecked and became the only survivor on a lonely island. He built a home (which he called his *castle*), kept goats, grew grain and made a boat. He had lived alone for many years.

**Scene 1 — the footprint.** One day around noon, walking towards his boat along the shore, Crusoe suddenly saw the clear print of a man's **bare foot** in the sand — toes, heel, every part.

**Scene 2 — shock.** He stood still as if struck by lightning. He listened and looked all around but saw and heard nothing. He climbed higher ground to look further, walked up and down the beach — but there was only that **one** footprint.

**Scene 3 — fear.** Terrified, he ran home to his fortress, looking behind him every few steps, imagining that every bush and tree was a man. He did not sleep that night. His mind raced: was it the devil? Was it a **savage** (the old novel's word for a stranger) from the mainland who had come in a canoe? Would they come back with others and eat him or destroy his crops and goats?

**Scene 4 — doubt.** After days of hiding, he began to think it might be his **own** footprint from an earlier walk. He went back to measure. He put his foot beside the print — and it was **much smaller** than the footprint! It was not his.

**Scene 5 — getting ready.** His fear returned. He decided to strengthen his castle: he planted more trees to hide it, built a second wall, and set up muskets (guns) through holes in the wall. He was ready to defend himself if anyone came.

**Themes:** fear of the unknown, loneliness, careful observation, and how the mind imagines dangers. (In the full novel, Crusoe later meets a man he names Friday.)

check.q: How did Crusoe prove the footprint wasn't his?
options: He compared his foot — the print was larger
check.why: He placed his foot beside the print and found the footprint was much bigger than his own.

sections.md:
**Words:** *shipwrecked* (survived a ship's sinking), *shore* (land by the sea), *thunderstruck* (shocked), *fortress/castle* (a strong, protected home), *terrified* (very scared), *notion* (idea), *arrant* (complete, utter), *dew* (tiny water drops on plants in the morning).

**Feelings words:** scared, nervous, puzzled, curious, relieved, brave.

**Grammar — simple past:** see → saw, run → ran, stand → stood, think → thought, go → went, find → found.

**Science link — shadows:** A shadow forms when an **opaque** object blocks light. Shadows are long in the morning and evening and shortest at noon. They fall on the side opposite the light.

**Writing:** Imagine you find a strange footprint near your school. Write a diary entry: what you saw, what you felt, what you did.

check.q: What is the past tense of 'think'?
check.why: 'Think' is an irregular verb; its past tense is 'thought'.

rd-school-c5-maths-a.ch1-the-fish-tale.title: The Fish Tale: Big Numbers on the Sea
rd-school-c5-maths-a.ch1-the-fish-tale.subtitle: Boats, kilograms, kilometres and rupees: the maths of a fishing village in Kerala

sections.md:
It is 4 o'clock in the morning at a harbour in Kerala. The sky is still dark, but the beach is busy. Fishermen push their boats into the waves, nets are loaded and engines cough into life. By evening the same boats will come back heavy with sardines, prawns and seer fish.

This chapter uses the life of a fishing village to practise **big numbers**: how far, how heavy, how fast and how much money. Fishing is real business, so every number matters to the families who live by the sea.

Kerala has a long coastline, about 590 km, and thousands of families earn their living from fishing. There are different kinds of boats:

- **Kattamaram (catamaran)**: logs tied together, moved by oars or a sail. It goes close to the shore.
- **Sailboat / small boat**: goes a bit further.
- **Motorboat**: has an engine, travels faster and further.
- **Big ship (trawler)**: goes very far out, stays for days and catches huge amounts.

The further a boat goes, the more fish it usually brings back, but the more fuel and money it needs.

sections.h: How far can each boat go?
sections.md:
Suppose:

| Boat | Goes out to sea (one way) |
|---|---|
| Kattamaram | 10 km |
| Sailboat | 20 km |
| Motorboat | 60 km |
| Big ship | 200 km |

The motorboat goes **6 times** as far as the kattamaram (60 ÷ 10 = 6). The big ship goes **10 times** as far as the sailboat (200 ÷ 20 = 10).

A round trip means going out *and* coming back, so double the distance: a motorboat's round trip is 60 + 60 = **120 km**.

**Speed.** If a motorboat travels 10 km in 1 hour, how long will it take to reach 60 km? 60 ÷ 10 = **6 hours**. If a sailboat moves 5 km in an hour, 20 km takes 20 ÷ 5 = **4 hours**.

> Did you know? Distances at sea are often measured in *nautical miles*. One nautical mile is about 1.85 km. In class we stick to kilometres.

check.q: A motorboat goes 60 km out to sea and comes back. What is the total distance?
check.why: A round trip is out and back, so 60 km + 60 km = 120 km.

sections.md:
Bigger boats carry more fish. Imagine one day's catch:

- A kattamaram brings **50 kg**.
- A motorboat brings **800 kg**.
- A big ship brings **10,000 kg**, which is the same as 10 tonnes (1 tonne = 1,000 kg).

How many kattamarams' catch equals one motorboat's? 800 ÷ 50 = **16**. How many motorboats' catch equals one big ship's? 10,000 ÷ 800 = 12.5, so about **12 and a half** motorboats.

Fish is sold in kg. If sardines sell at ₹120 per kg, then 50 kg brings 50 × 120 = **₹6,000**.

**Reading big numbers.** Indian place value groups digits as ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, ten lakhs, crores:

| Crore | Ten lakh | Lakh | Ten thousand | Thousand | Hundred | Ten | One |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | 1 | 2 | 5 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

That number is 1,25,000, read as *one lakh twenty-five thousand*. The international way writes it as 125,000 (*one hundred twenty-five thousand*).

check.q: How is 3,40,500 read?
options: Three lakh forty thousand five hundred
check.why: In Indian grouping, 3 is in the lakhs place and 40 in the thousands, so it reads three lakh forty thousand five hundred.

sections.md:
A lakh is hard to imagine. Let's build it up with fish!

- 10 fish in a basket.
- 10 baskets = 100 fish in a box.
- 10 boxes = **1,000** fish on a boat.
- 10 boats = **10,000** fish at the harbour.
- 10 harbours' catch = **1,00,000** fish — one lakh!

So **1 lakh = 100 thousands = 1,000 hundreds**.

Other ways to feel a lakh:

- If you count one number every second without stopping, counting to 1 lakh takes 1,00,000 seconds — that's more than **27 hours**! (1 hour = 3,600 seconds; 1,00,000 ÷ 3,600 ≈ 27.8.)
- A stack of 1 lakh ₹1 coins would be many times taller than a house.

**Comparing numbers.** Which is bigger, 98,999 or 1,00,000? The second has more digits (6 vs 5), so it is bigger — it is just **1 more** than 99,999.

**Writing in expanded form.** 2,46,305 = 2,00,000 + 40,000 + 6,000 + 300 + 0 + 5.

check.q: How many thousands make one lakh?
check.why: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 = 100 × 1,000, so 100 thousands make a lakh.

sections.md:
A fisherman, let's call him Raghavan, wants a motorboat. It costs **₹2,50,000** (two lakh fifty thousand). Where does the money come from?

Many fishermen join a **cooperative**, a group that helps its members get loans and sell fish at a fair price. Suppose Raghavan pays ₹50,000 himself and borrows the rest:

2,50,000 − 50,000 = **₹2,00,000** borrowed.

If he pays back ₹10,000 every month, it takes 2,00,000 ÷ 10,000 = **20 months**, without counting interest.

**Fuel cost.** A motorboat may use about 4 litres of diesel each hour. A 12-hour trip (6 hours out, 6 back) needs 4 × 12 = **48 litres**. At ₹90 per litre that's 48 × 90 = **₹4,320**.

So a trip only pays if the fish sells for more than the fuel, the workers' share and the boat repairs. That's the *real* fish tale: earning is not the same as profit.

check.q: A boat uses 5 litres of diesel per hour on a 10-hour trip. How many litres does it use?
check.why: Multiply litres per hour by hours: 5 × 10 = 50 litres.

sections.md:
The cooperative keeps a record of one motorboat's catch for a week:

| Day | Catch (kg) |
|---|---|
| Mon | 640 |
| Tue | 815 |
| Wed | 0 (storm — no fishing) |
| Thu | 1,120 |
| Fri | 760 |
| Sat | 905 |

**Total**: 640 + 815 = 1,455; + 0 = 1,455; + 1,120 = 2,575; + 760 = 3,335; + 905 = **4,240 kg**. That's 4 tonnes 240 kg.

**Best day**: Thursday (1,120 kg). **Difference** between best and worst fishing day (ignoring the storm): 1,120 − 640 = **480 kg**.

Why no fishing on Wednesday? Rough seas are dangerous. Fishermen listen to **weather warnings** on radio and mobile phones. During the monsoon there is also a **fishing ban** period of some weeks, which lets fish breed and keeps boats safe.

> **Did you know?** Fishermen today use GPS and phone apps to find fish shoals and check the weather — maths and technology at sea!

Nets are bought by weight or length. If a net weighs 2 kg per 100 metres, then 1,000 metres (1 km) of net weighs 2 × 10 = **20 kg**.

**Estimation** helps when exact numbers are hard. If 9 boats each bring roughly 780 kg, estimate: about 10 boats × 800 kg = 8,000 kg. The exact answer is 9 × 780 = 7,020 kg, so our estimate gives the right size of the answer.

**Fish change price.** In the morning when boats arrive, fish is fresh and costly. By evening the price drops, because ice and storage cost money. Selling quickly matters, which is why fish is packed in ice and sent by truck and train to cities like Kochi, Bengaluru and Chennai.

check.why: Round to 50 × 20 = 1,000; the exact answer, 1,029, is close to that.

sections.h: Did you know? Cooperatives and fairness
sections.md:
Earlier, many fishermen had to sell to middlemen who paid them very little. Cooperatives let fishermen sell together and share profits fairly. Maths turns into fairness here: if 8 fishermen share ₹24,000 from a catch, each gets 24,000 ÷ 8 = **₹3,000**. If the owner keeps half first, there's only ₹12,000 left to share, so each gets ₹1,500. Always ask *who gets what share*.

**Talk about it:** Have you visited a fish market or any market? How do sellers decide prices? Why might prices be higher in a city than at the harbour?

parts.md: Ammu's father's boat came in at sunset, and Ammu ran down the sand with her notebook. 'Seven boxes of sardines, Achan! Each box about 30 kg.' She scribbled: 7 × 30 = 210 kg.

At the auction the price was ₹110 a kg. 'That's 210 × 110,' she muttered — 210 × 100 = 21,000, plus 210 × 10 = 2,100 — 'twenty-three thousand one hundred rupees!' The auctioneer laughed. 'This girl is faster than my calculator.'

But Achan reminded her of the diesel: ₹4,500. And the three helpers' shares. Ammu subtracted, frowned, and wrote PROFIT in big letters. 'Next time,' she said, 'we sell in the morning, when the price is high.'

A round trip is twice the one-way distance.
Time = distance ÷ speed.
1 tonne = 1,000 kg.

Numbers can be written in expanded form, e.g. 2,46,305 = 2,00,000 + 40,000 + 6,000 + 300 + 5.

rd-school-c5-maths-a.ch2-shapes-and-angl.title: Shapes and Angles: Corners Everywhere
rd-school-c5-maths-a.ch2-shapes-and-angl.subtitle: Right, sharp and wide angles, plus how to make an angle tester and read the clock's angles

sections.md:
Look around your room. The corner of your book, where two walls meet, the tip of a slice of pizza, the hands of a clock: each one is an **angle**.

An angle forms where **two straight lines meet at a point**. The point is the **vertex** and the two lines are the **arms**. The *size* of an angle is how far one arm has turned away from the other. It is **not** how long the arms are. A tiny angle drawn with long arms is still tiny.

Shapes are made of lines and corners:

| Shape | Sides | Corners (angles) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 3 |
| Square / rectangle | 4 | 4 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 5 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 6 |
| Circle | no straight sides | no corners |

Count the sides and you know the corners: a closed shape made of straight lines always has the same number of each.
keyTerms: Vertex — the point where the two arms meet
Arms — the two lines that make an angle
Angle — the amount of turn between two arms

sections.md:
Take a box of matchsticks (used ones are fine). Make these and count the angles:

- **3 sticks** → a triangle with 3 angles, all equal and sharp.
- **4 sticks** → a square (4 right angles) — or push it sideways to get a 'pushed square' (rhombus) with 2 sharp and 2 wide angles. Same sticks, different angles!
- **5 sticks** → a pentagon or a house shape (a square with a pointed roof).
- **6 sticks** → a hexagon, like a honeycomb cell, with 6 wide angles.

Now try **letters**: make L, T, V, N, Z, E, M, W. Which letter uses right angles only? (E, F, H, L, T.) Which use only sharp angles? (V, N, Z, M, W.)

This shows something important: **the same sides can make different angles**. A shape is decided by both its sides and its angles.

> **Did you know?** Bees build hexagon cells because hexagons fit together with no gaps and use the least wax.

check.q: You push a matchstick square sideways. What changes?
check.why: The sides stay the same, but the corners stop being right angles: two become sharp and two become wide.

sections.md:
The most important angle is the **right angle**, the corner of a page or of a square tile. It is a *quarter turn*.

Compared with a right angle:

- **Less than a right angle** (sharp, pointy, like a pizza slice or the beak of a bird): this is an *acute* angle.
- **Exactly a right angle** (square corner).
- **More than a right angle** but less than a straight line (wide open, like a reclining chair): this is an *obtuse* angle.

A straight line makes **two right angles** together, a half turn.

**Make an angle tester.** Fold any piece of paper in half, then fold it in half again so the first fold lies on itself. The corner you get is a perfect right angle. Hold it against corners at home: is your door a right angle? The bottom of a window? The tip of a samosa?

check.q: Which is the best example of an angle smaller than a right angle?
options: The tip of a pizza slice
An open laptop leaning far back
check.why: A pizza slice tip is narrower than a square corner, so its angle is less than a right angle.

sections.md:
Capital letters hide angles:

- **L** has one right angle.
- **V** has one angle less than a right angle.
- **E** and **F** are full of right angles.
- **N**, **M**, **W**, **Z** have sharp angles.
- **O** and **S** have no corners at all, just curves.

In shapes: every corner of a **square** and of a **rectangle** is a right angle. A triangle can have *at most one* right angle. A triangle can have all three angles sharp, or one right angle, or one wide angle, but never two wide ones, because the arms would never meet!

> Did you know? Builders use a large set-square or a string with knots (a 3-4-5 triangle) to check that walls meet at a right angle.

check.q: Which capital letter has no angles at all?
check.why: O is made of one curved line with no straight arms meeting, so it has no angles.

sections.md:
Pick up a shape and sort its corners. Here is a detective table for some common shapes:

| Shape | Sharp | Right | Wide |
|---|---|---|---|
| Square | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| Rectangle | 0 | 4 | 0 |
| Set-square (triangle) | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| Equal-sided triangle | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| Rhombus (pushed square) | 2 | 0 | 2 |
| Regular hexagon | 0 | 0 | 6 |
| House shape (5 sides) | 1 | 2 | 2 |

Check the house shape: the two bottom corners are right angles, the roof tip is sharp, and the two corners where the roof meets the walls are wide. 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 corners for 5 sides. ✔

**On dot paper.** Join dots to draw a shape with exactly 1 right angle, then one with 2 right angles, then one with 2 wide angles. Can you draw a 4-sided shape with **3 right angles** but not 4? (Try — you'll find the fourth is forced to be right too!)

check.q: How many wide angles does a regular hexagon have?
check.why: All six corners of a regular hexagon are more than a right angle, so it has 6 wide angles.

sections.md:
A clock is an angle machine. When the minute hand moves from 12 to 3, it turns a quarter of a full circle, a **right angle**.

| Time | Angle between hands |
|---|---|
| 3:00 | right angle |
| 9:00 | right angle |
| 6:00 | straight line (two right angles) |
| 1:00 | less than a right angle |
| 5:00 | more than a right angle |
| 12:00 | hands on top of each other, no gap |

In one hour the minute hand makes a **full turn**, which is four right angles. In 15 minutes it makes one right angle. In 30 minutes it makes a half turn.

**Degrees.** Mathematicians split a full turn into 360 small parts called **degrees** (°). A right angle = 90°, a straight line = 180°, a full turn = 360°. Each number on the clock is 360 ÷ 12 = **30°** from the next.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='150' r='130' fill='#fffde7' stroke='#795548' stroke-width='8'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='20' text-anchor='middle'><text x='150' y='45'>12</text><text x='262' y='157'>3</text><text x='150' y='270'>6</text><text x='38' y='157'>9</text></g><path d='M150 150 L150 40 A110 110 0 0 1 260 150 Z' fill='#81c784' opacity='0.5'/><line x1='150' y1='150' x2='150' y2='60' stroke='#333' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0 150 150' to='360 150 150' dur='12s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='150' y1='150' x2='225' y2='150' stroke='#c62828' stroke-width='8' stroke-linecap='round'/><circle cx='150' cy='150' r='8' fill='#333'/></svg>
fig.caption: At 3 o'clock the hands make a right angle (shaded). The black minute hand keeps turning: one full turn is four right angles.
fig.alt: Clock face with a shaded quarter and a rotating minute hand

check.q: How many right angles does the minute hand turn through in one hour?
check.why: One hour is a full turn, and a full turn is made of four right angles (4 × 90° = 360°).

sections.md:
- **Doors**: a door that is half-open makes an angle with the wall. Open wider and the angle grows.
- **Scissors**: as you open them, the blades make bigger and bigger angles.
- **Cricket**: a fielder throws best when the arm makes a wide angle. A ramp for a wheelchair must have a *small* angle so it's easy to climb.
- **Roads**: a crossroads makes right angles; a Y-junction makes sharp angles.
- **Kolam and rangoli**: many patterns are built from lines meeting at equal angles around a centre dot.

**Turning in directions.** Facing north and turning a right angle clockwise, you face east. Two right angles: south. Three: west. Four: back to north. That's a full turn.

To compare two angles, place one on top of the other so the vertices match and one arm lies along the other. The angle whose free arm sticks out further is the **bigger** angle.

A quick way to draw a right angle: use the corner of your ruler or set-square, or draw along a line and up the side of your geometry box.

**Body angles game.** Stand straight and stretch one arm forward. Your partner calls 'sharp!', 'right!', 'wide!' or 'straight!' and you move your other arm to make that angle with the first. Swap roles.

**Angles in a fan.** Fold a paper fan. Each fold makes a small angle; open the fan wide and the angles add up to a half turn.

check.q: You face east and turn two right angles. Which way are you facing now?
check.why: Two right angles make a half turn, and a half turn from east points you west.

workedExamples.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 20 minutes?
Angle between hands at 2:00?
workedExamples.answer: 60°, less than a right angle

workedExamples.q: How many right angles are there in a rectangle?
steps: Each corner is a right angle

workedExamples.q: Angle between hands at 4:00?
workedExamples.answer: 120°, a wide angle

workedExamples.q: How many right angles does the minute hand turn from 7:15 to 8:00?
workedExamples.answer: 3 right angles

summary: An angle forms where two arms meet at a vertex.
Angle size is the amount of turn, not arm length.
A right angle is a quarter turn (90°).
Angles less than a right angle are sharp (acute); more than a right angle are wide (obtuse).
A straight line is two right angles (180°); a full turn is four (360°).
A folded paper makes a right-angle tester.
The same sides can make different angles (square vs pushed square).
Squares and rectangles have four right angles; a triangle can have at most one.
Letters like E, F, H, L, T have right angles; V, N, Z, M, W have sharp ones.
Clock numbers are 30° apart; 15 minutes is a right angle for the minute hand.
practice: Draw an angle smaller than a right angle and one larger than a right angle.
Name 5 objects at home that have right angles.
Which capital letters in your name have angles? Sort them into sharp, right and wide.
Make a house shape with 5 matchsticks and count its sharp, right and wide angles.
What angle do clock hands make at 6:00? At 4:00?
How far does the minute hand turn in 45 minutes, in right angles?
Can a triangle have two right angles? Explain.
Facing north, you turn three right angles clockwise. Which way do you face?
Make an angle tester from paper and list what you tested.

rd-school-c5-maths-a.ch3-how-many-square.title: How Many Squares? Measuring Space by Counting
rd-school-c5-maths-a.ch3-how-many-square.subtitle: Squared paper, half squares, stamps and tiles: discover area by counting

sections.md:
Meera and Kabir each drew a rangoli on the courtyard floor. Meera's is long and thin, Kabir's is fat and short. Who used more space?

You can't tell just by looking. But if both rangolis are drawn on a floor of square tiles, you can **count the tiles each one covers**. Whoever covers more squares used more space.

The space a flat shape covers is its **area**. In this chapter we measure area the simplest way, by counting squares. Each square is one **unit**. We use squares because they fit together with no gaps and no overlaps, so counting them is fair.

We'll explore: counting full and half squares, shapes with the same area, a dot game, halving a square, stamps and tiles, faces of a matchbox, hidden squares in grids, and estimating the area of your own hand.

On squared paper (1 cm squares), draw shapes by joining the dots. Then count:

1. Count the **full squares** inside.
2. Look for squares cut exactly in half along a diagonal. **Two halves make one full square.**
3. Add them up.

Example: a shape has 6 full squares and 4 half squares. Area = 6 + 4 ÷ 2 = 6 + 2 = **8 squares**.

For curvy shapes, like a leaf traced on squared paper, use this rule:
- Count a square if **more than half** of it is inside the shape.
- Ignore it if **less than half** is inside.

This gives a good *estimate* of the area.
